questions.question: Which of these is the best definition of "financial literacy"?
options: Being able to do math quickly in your head
Knowing how to earn, save, spend, borrow, and invest money wisely
questions.explanation: Financial literacy is the whole package of money skills — earning, saving, spending, borrowing, and investing — not a single metric.

questions.question: Which of these is a SMART financial goal?
options: "I want to save $1,500 for a summer trip by June 1st"
"I should probably start investing at some point"
"I'll save whatever's left at the end of the month"
questions.explanation: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Vague wishes don't move your bank account.

questions.question: The average American sees approximately how many ads per year?
questions.explanation: Streaming, social feeds, billboards, TV, product placements, sponsorships — it all adds up to roughly 1.5M touchpoints per year. That constant pressure is a big reason "wants" quietly become "needs."

questions.question: In the classic 50/30/20 budget, what goes in the 20%?
questions.explanation: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% future-you (savings + debt payoff). The 20% is how you actually build wealth.

questions.question: What percentage of Americans have set a formal budget for 2026?
questions.explanation: Just over half of Americans have set a formal 2026 budget — up from 46% in 2025. Budgeting adoption is rising, but almost half of adults still wing it every month.

questions.question: What's the #1 reason people fail to stick to their budget?
options: Unexpected "emergency" costs — medical bills, car repairs, etc.
questions.explanation: More than half of adults across every age group say surprise expenses are what actually derail their budget. This is exactly why an emergency fund matters — it absorbs the hit so your plan keeps working.

questions.question: "Lifestyle creep" is the tendency for your spending to…
options: Stay flat no matter how much you earn
Rise as your income rises, so you save less than you expected
Drop automatically when you get a raise
questions.explanation: As income grows, spending often grows with it. Lifestyle creep is why high earners sometimes still feel broke.

questions.question: How many months of living expenses should a solid emergency fund cover?
questions.explanation: 3–6 months of essential expenses covers most real surprises — job loss, medical bills, car repair — without forcing you to tap credit cards or sell investments at a bad time.

questions.question: Which of these is MOST likely to quietly drain your bank account over a year WITHOUT you noticing?
questions.explanation: The one-time purchases hurt once. A forgotten subscription hits every month forever — and most people have three to five of them.

questions.question: What's the MOST important rule for managing a credit card?
options: Always use the card with the highest rewards rate
Pay the minimum balance every month
Pay the full statement balance every month
Close old cards to protect your credit
questions.explanation: Pay in full, every month, no exceptions. That's how you keep the rewards, build credit history, and avoid the 20%+ interest trap. Every other "rule" is a distant second.

questions.question: What percentage of American credit cardholders DON'T pay their balance in full every month?
questions.explanation: Roughly half of Americans carry a balance month to month — paying interest on past purchases instead of keeping the rewards. The "pay in full" rule is simple; actually doing it puts you ahead of half the country.

questions.question: Which factor has the BIGGEST impact on your credit score?
options: The brand of credit card you have
Whether you pay your bills on time
How many credit cards you own
questions.explanation: Payment history is about 35% of your FICO score — the single biggest lever. Income doesn't show up on your credit score at all.

questions.question: Who ends up with more money at 65 — Player A, who invests $100/month from age 25 to 35 and then STOPS, or Player B, who invests $100/month from age 35 until 65?
options: Player A, even though she only invested for 10 years
Player B, he invested 3x as long
It depends on how high the fees are
questions.explanation: Player A ends up with about $407K; Player B with about $226K. Starting early almost always beats saving more later. Time > amount.

questions.question: Why do most beginner investors start with an index fund instead of picking individual stocks?
options: They give you a slice of hundreds of companies at once, spreading risk
Only professional investors are allowed to buy individual stocks
questions.explanation: An S&P 500 index fund owns 500 companies at once — if any one of them tanks, it barely moves your portfolio. Low fees + built-in diversification = why this is the default starting point.

questions.question: A Gonzaga athlete who lives in California earns $10,000 from an NIL deal with a Spokane business. Washington has no state income tax. Does the athlete owe state tax on that money?
options: No — the deal happened in Washington, and Washington has no income tax
Yes — California taxes its residents on ALL income, including money earned out of state
Only if the deal is over $25,000
Only federal tax applies to NIL
questions.explanation: Your home state generally taxes all your income — even money you earn somewhere else. Most college athletes are still residents of their home state during school, so a California athlete owes CA state tax on that NIL deal even though Washington itself takes nothing.
